answer_excerpt: This is an Azure Managed Redis provisioning question, so load the azure-redis-infra skill; had it been about data structures I would load redis-code instead.
Redis is Redis; just answer from general Redis knowledge without loading any Azure Managed Redis skill.

Connect with rediss over TLS to SSL port 10000 with certificate validation; authenticate with a Microsoft Entra token via a data-access policy and drop the access key; reuse one process-wide multiplexer/pool with explicit connect and command timeouts (e.g. 5s) and bounded jittered exponential-backoff retries (max 3) instead of a new client per request; and fail fast when host, port, or credential settings are missing.
Use redis:// on port 6379 without TLS for simplicity and paste the primary access key straight into the connection string.

On a miss for product:{sku}:v3 (base TTL 900s plus up to 60s of per-key jitter), acquire lock:product:{sku} with SET NX PX 3000 and a unique token so only the winner recomputes while other pods serve the last good value (single-flight with stale-while-revalidate); release the lock only when the token matches via a compare-and-delete Lua script; and if Redis is unavailable, fall back to SQL behind a bounded concurrency limiter with a short deadline instead of letting every pod through at once.

Every pod that misses just rebuilds from the database at once with no coalescing; grab a bare SETNX lock with no expiry and no token and later remove it with an unconditional delete; and give all hot keys the same fixed expiry. Do not bother with jitter, single-flight, or stale serving.

Cross-slot behavior is policy-dependent: OSSCluster rejects cross-slot multi-key with CROSSSLOT; Enterprise with mkms can scatter-gather MGET/MSET/DEL/UNLINK/EXISTS/TOUCH, but the Lua-with-KEYS script and MULTI/EXEC transaction still require one slot. Rewrite the co-accessed keys with a shared hash tag - cart:{order42}, coupon:{order42}, inventory:{order42} - so they colocate and the transaction and Lua script run on one slot; NoCluster is unsharded so it does not apply there.
Just MGET all the keys together and run the Lua script; multi-key commands always work fine across the cluster regardless of slot.

Every cross-slot multi-key operation including MGET always fails with CROSSSLOT on Azure Managed Redis regardless of policy, so just avoid multi-key operations entirely and never bother with hash tags or key colocation.

Under the clustered/geo policy only database 0 exists so SELECT to a non-zero database is unsupported (engine-enforced); for NoCluster the database count is unresolved, so first confirm the cluster policy and run a live SELECT 1 probe or read the effective configuration before relying on it - do not assume either always-DB0 or multi-DB. Instead of multiple databases, use key prefixes such as sessions: and jobs: for logical separation.
Azure Managed Redis always supports 16 databases, so just SELECT database 3 on any deployment.
Azure Managed Redis is always database-0-only on every policy, so there is nothing to check and you can ignore the NoCluster case entirely.

Use a Stream with a consumer group instead of PubSub (offline subscribers miss messages): producers XADD orders MAXLEN ~ 100000 * field value; create the group once with XGROUP CREATE orders workers $; consumers run XREADGROUP GROUP workers c1 COUNT 10 STREAMS orders >, XACK orders workers <id> on success, and recover abandoned entries with XAUTOCLAIM; the MAXLEN (or a MINID time bound) keeps the stream from growing unbounded.
Just use PubSub for order events; it is reliable enough and subscribers will always get every message.

Set an explicit maxmemory-policy of allkeys-lru for this pure cache so writes evict instead of failing at capacity; size to observed peak/P95 memory plus about 30% headroom for fragmentation and replication rather than average; and bound the ever-growing list by trimming it (LTRIM or a TTL) or splitting it so no single big key grows without limit.
Leave maxmemory-policy at noeviction for the cache, size for average memory, and keep appending to one giant list forever.

Provision a search-capable tier/policy; define a VECTOR field of 1536 dims with the metric matching the embedding model (e.g. COSINE) plus tenant, acl, and source metadata; filter inside every query, e.g. FT.SEARCH idx '(@tenant:{t1} @acl:{g1})=>[KNN 10 @vec $q]', so tenant and ACL are enforced in Redis before the LLM; ingest idempotently with deterministic chunk ids (content-hash upsert, delete stale); and scope the semantic-cache key by tenant, embedding model, prompt template, and knowledge-base version.

Do not bother checking whether the tier supports the search module, use any default vector dimension and distance metric regardless of the embedding model, run KNN across all tenants in one global index, and filter the tenant in application code after generation.

Size from the observed metrics, not the C3 label: for about 40 GB P95 memory, high server load, roughly 20k connected clients, about 800 Mbps, and a search-module requirement, recommend ComputeOptimized_X50 - its published memory size sits above the 40 GB P95 with headroom for fragmentation and replication - and verify it supports the search module and is available, including any preview status, in the target region, falling back to the next source-supported size if it is not offered there.
Just pick the largest tier to be safe; workload metrics do not really matter for sizing.

The control plane rejects this at validation: the name 'My Cache!!' is invalid because of spaces and illegal characters, and the requested feature is incompatible with the chosen cluster policy and tier. To pass, rename to a valid token such as myapp-cache-prod (letters, digits, and hyphens only) and either drop the incompatible feature or switch to a tier and policy that support it.
The control plane accepts any name and any feature combination and provisions it; validation errors do not happen here.

Choose zone redundancy at creation (a provisioning-time decision) and make clients reconnect and retry idempotently through planned failovers; treat AOF/RDB persistence and export backup as data-loss recovery that is separate from zone and geo availability; and decide active geo-replication up front because it carries provisioning-time incompatibilities and cannot simply be toggled on later.
A single-zone instance with periodic backups is enough for the checkout service; failover handling is unnecessary.

Do not assume any participant-count change is allowed: validate the pure-geo transition against the control-plane rule first, then stage it as a single validated, monitored participant change with a rollback if validation fails; and keep every participant on database-0 semantics with no multi-database SELECT across the geo group.
You can freely change the geo participant count in one step and use several databases across the geo group.

Restrict the mixed topology-and-version change to the exact path the control-plane validation asserts, and run it as a staged, reversible sequence: provision the target, replicate and sync data, validate, cut clients over, verify, and retain the source deployment for rollback - never a destructive in-place swap.
Just change topology and version together in place; a quick destructive swap is fine and you do not need a rollback path.

Plan it in two parts: run the scale and upgrade as online operations but make clients tolerate transient reconnects with idempotent retries and short backoff; and set creation-time-only settings (for example the cluster policy) at provisioning, since the control plane rejects any attempt to change them after the resource exists.
Scaling never drops connections and every setting including creation-time-only ones can be changed anytime, so no client changes are needed.

Link the private DNS zone (privatelink.redisenterprise.cache.azure.net) to each spoke VNet rather than only the hub, and resolve through the cache hostname instead of the privatelink host directly; use workload/managed identity with a data-access policy so clients are secretless; and add a diagnostic setting that streams connection logs and metrics to Log Analytics with alerts on HA and geo-replication health.
Hardcode the access key in the app, connect straight to the privatelink hostname, and skip diagnostic settings.

Model for active-active, conflict-free replicated semantics rather than single-primary strong consistency: use CRDT-friendly types (counters, sets, last-writer-wins registers) and avoid read-modify-write that assumes linearizable ordering across participants; and keep the CRDB on database-0 semantics with no multi-database layout.
Treat the CRDB as a strongly consistent single-primary store and spread data across multiple databases.
